title: A Study of Housing Insecurity Risk Factors Across the Rural-Urban Continuum
content: Housing insecurity is a critical aspect of understanding public health. To date, most work concerning housing insecurity focuses on urban environments with little research on rural conditions and the potential differences that exist between these environment. This leads to a fundamental question: how does housing insecurity change as we progress across the rural-urban continuum? To tackle this question, we considered several measures derived from the 2020-2024 5-year American Community Estimates and performed cluster analysis and association rules mining on a set of seven risk factors. We then further broke the analysis down based on the RUCA codes established by the US Department of Agriculture at the census tract geometry level. The results show that various housing insecurity factors predict others to varying degrees, based on rural/suburban/urban characteristics, with flow destinations (more urban settings) having different interaction profiles than flow providers (more suburban settings) and the most rural locales. The RUCA code provides a consistent pattern based on flow-rate to a central location. Connections to the extant literature about predictive mechanisms between subfacets are made. These differences and patterns have implications for policy and remediation, suggesting a typological approach to housing insecurity services based on aspects of the rural-urban continuum (a geospatial concept) and critical demographic data (a socioeconomic concept).
